name: Pattani Malay
catalog_citation: Nawanit Yupho. 1989. Consonant clusters and stress rules in Pattani Malay. Mon-Khmer Studies 15:125-137.
catalog_locator: pp.133-135, section 6 and section 7 'A Complete Set of Stress Rules' (also abstract p.125)
catalog_quote: It can now be seen that there is a relation between geminate consonants and the primary stress; that is, words with initial geminate consonants automatically have the primary stress on the initial syllable. This is in contrast with words with initial simple consonants, where the primary stress would normally fall on the final syllable. ... (1.) Every word with an initial single consonant has a syllable that bears a primary stress. If the word is monosyllabic, it bears primary stress. In a word of more than one syllable the primary stress is on the last syllable. Thus if the word is disyllabic, the primary stress will be on the second syllable, or if the word is trisyllabic, the primary stress will be on the third syllable. The rest of the syllables will bear a secondary (weak) stress or no stress, depending on the further conditions which will be mentioned in rules 2a and 2b. ... (2a.) …

sources.citation: Wu, Jiang. 2023. Malayic varieties of Kelantan and Terengganu. LOT 651 (Leiden PhD). [already]
sources.quote: For Kelantan Malay (same glottocode, Malaysian side): 'KM has no phonemic stress' ... CVCV words 'generally have stress on the penultimate syllable. When the penultimate syllable has a schwa, stress falls on the final syllable instead'; coda /ʔ/ syllables attract stress; 'in words with initial geminates, stress always falls on the initial syllable'; explicitly contrasts this with Yupho 1989: 'In KM, however, words do not have ultimate stress by default.' Impressionistic, flagged as tentative by the author.

sources.citation: Abramson, Arthur S. 2004. Toward prosodic contrast: Suai and Pattani Malay. Proc. International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2004), Beijing, 1-4.
sources.quote: Instrumental: in words with long (geminate) initial consonants the first syllable has higher peak amplitude (ratio ~3x) and higher F0; perception experiments show F0+amplitude on syllable 1 cue the geminate. Conclusion: Pattani Malay is shifting 'from word-initial distinctive consonant length, to a kind of prosodic salience' possibly 'phonemic stress or accent'. Says nothing about default (singleton-initial) word-stress position.

sources.citation: Abramson, Arthur S. 2003. Acoustic cues to word-initial stop length in Pattani Malay. Proc. 15th ICPhS, Barcelona, 387-390.
sources.quote: 'Listening suggested greater salience on the first syllable of words with a long plosive, and higher amplitude and fundamental frequency were found on such first syllables' ... 'the length distinction as such is still present in Pattani Malay but is undergoing a transition to a system of accentual prominence on the first syllable of words'. Instrumental support for the geminate-initial => initial-prominence half of the coding; silent on default final stress.
